The widespread contamination of industrial wastewater with synthetic dyes presents a serious environmental challenge, impacting ecosystems, water quality, and public health. Developing 3D-printed polymeric resin composites embedded with g-C
nanosheet scaffolds that were fabricated by stereolithography (SLA) technique for wastewater treatment applications. In this research, we enhanced the physicochemical characteristics of bulk g-C
via direct thermal delamination. Structural analysis using X-ray diffraction (XRD) confirmed the crystalline phase of g-C
, and Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) revealed the nanosheets' morphology, with an average thickness conducive to high surface activity. The adsorption behavior of both bulk g-C

scaffolds was evaluated in the dark for 16 hours to ensure the attainment of adsorption equilibrium. Photocatalytic testing was performed under UV light (λ = 365 nm). After 8 hours of UV exposure, the dye removal efficiency of the 3D-printed composites against MB dyes reached 78%, 83%, 84%, and 86%, respectively, demonstrating their potential for effective dye removal. The results highlight the effectiveness of 3D-printed g-C

/polymeric resin composites as a viable solution for dye-contaminated wastewater, advancing sustainable treatment methods and contributing to environmental conservation and cleaner industrial processes

Industrial wastewater frequently contains synthetic dyes and aromatic pollutants that are resistant to biodegradation, making effective treatment challenging

. Methylene blue aqueous dye solutions are widely utilized within the material, paper, leather, pharmaceutical, and cosmetic industries, and when discharged into water sources, they can cause serious risks
. More than 10,000 dyes and pigments have been used in production factories, with approximately 7 x 105 tons of synthetic dyes generated annually
Dye wastewater includes a variety of contaminants, including dangerous adhesives, bases, or salts acidic substances, and auxiliaries that are teratogenic for cancer-causing, and exotic foods

. These characteristics may cause symptoms related to asthma, skin irritations, eye burns, and allergic conjunctivitis in humans. Consequently, the removal of organic dyes from wastewater has become increasingly important. A variety of methods for treating dye waste have been produced including membrane filtering, chemical deposition, and adsorption. Unfortunately, the treatments mainly remove the molecule of dye from water bodies to other materials such as adsorption compounds sediments, or membranes, rather than removing current dyes. Hybrid approaches such as combining electrocoagulation with photocatalysis have also shown improved dye removal efficiency in textile effluents
. Recently, the graphite-layered double hydroxides (LDH/GP) composites can effectively adsorb malachite green dye from wastewater, achieving high removal efficiency and reusability
. Combining electrocoagulation with supported photocatalysis can achieve up to 90% dye removal from batik textile wastewater with high COD levels

. However, these techniques are complex and require substantial financial investments, making them less suitable for small-scale applications. In contrast, photodegradation treatment provides a promising method for entirely removing the color from wastewater. When dangerous dye molecules are exposed to photodegradation, they break down into less toxic particles or molecules, and they completely disintegrate into water (H
). As a result, photodegradation has become an efficient method for wastewater treatment

This research focuses on creating composite materials tailored for efficient dye removal, utilizing 3D printing to fabricate wastewater treatment composites composed of polymer resins, adsorbents, and catalysts. In this study, we synthesized
nanosheets through a thermal oxidation technique. The influence of thermal exfoliation conditions on the structural characteristics and photocatalytic properties of
was thoroughly evaluated. This method enhanced the photocatalytic efficiency of porous

via the thermal polymerization of melamine. The process required two distinct heating phases, leading to improved functionality. It was observed that raising the exfoliation temperature to 560 °C significantly improved the specific surface area, reaching 62 m²/g. Higher temperatures resulted in smaller particle sizes and thinner nanosheet structures. The transformation from bulk

to nanosheets was identified as a sequential oxidation process accompanied by the separation of layers, contributing to the reduced particle dimensions and an increased energy band gap. This research introduces an innovative method for developing nanostructures and optimizing the electronic properties of

to enhance its photocatalytic activity in degrading methylene blue (MB). Furthermore, the nanosheets demonstrated excellent stability under repeated irradiation, retaining high photocatalytic efficiency across multiple reaction cycles. This technology facilitates wastewater treatment through both adsorption and photocatalytic approaches.

The photocatalytic performance of 3D-printed bulk g-C

nanosheet scaffolds was assessed by examining the degradation of methylene blue (MB) in water-based solutions under exposure to UV light. During the experiment, 3D-printed catalyst samples were immersed in 100 mL of a 0.01 mg L⁻¹ aqueous MB solution in a glass container. The adsorption experiment was carried out in the dark for 24 hours, followed by UV irradiation for 8 hours. Throughout the reaction, 3 mL of the solution was extracted at hourly intervals using a syringe to monitor the MB concentration. The removal efficiency of MB dyes was evaluated after the 24 hours adsorption period by exposing the dye containing solution to UV light (λ = 365 nm) for 8 hours. To evaluate the degradation kinetics, the values of ln(C/C₀) were plotted as a function of irradiation time (t), where C₀ is the initial dye concentration and C is the concentration at a specific reaction time. The resulting linear trend indicates that the degradation process fits a pseudo–first-order kinetic model,

where k represents the apparent rate constant (min⁻¹). The pseudo first order nature of the reaction implies that the degradation rate is predominantly governed by the dye concentration, rather than by the simultaneous interaction of multiple reactants as seen in second-order systems. The kinetic behavior is observed in photocatalytic degradation processes, where the reaction is primarily driven by the generation and activity of reactive species such as hydroxyl radicals (OH) and superoxide radicals (O₂⁻) at the catalyst surface, which facilitate the breakdown of organic dye molecules.

w:r.w:t: The effectiveness of charge separation and the recombination of photo-excited electrons and holes in photocatalysts is related to the photoluminescence (PL) intensity.
Figure 11 displays the PL spectra of bulk g-C
C) NSs nanosheets, under excitation at 350 nm. The PL intensity of the bulk g-C
is larger than those of the exfoliated CN samples, indicating reduced radiative recombination. The efficiency of

separating and recombining photogenerated electrons and holes in photocatalysts is correlated with the intensity of photoluminescence (PL). The layered architecture of g-C₃N₄ promoted rapid charge recombination due to extended interlayer migration pathways. Exfoliation into few-layer nanosheets mitigated this limitation by confining the material in two dimensions, which shortened the diffusion length for charges to reach the surface
. This morphological change, coupled with an enlarged surface area and a greater abundance of accessible nitrogen sites, synergistically improved charge separation efficiency.
Overall, UV and PL spectra demonstrate that
nanosheets display improved photocatalytic characteristics compared to bulk g-C

. This enhancement can be ascribed to various factors, including the wider spectrum of visible light absorption by the nanosheets, the greater presence of active surface areas, and the inclusion of structural imperfections within the nanosheets. These characteristics enhance the production efficiency of electron-hole pairs when exposed to light and reduce their recombination during the charge transfer mechanism.

Reusability and Stability of the Photocatalyst Scaffold

To investigate the practical applicability of the scaffolds, their reusability for dye removal was examined. After each use, the g-C₃N₄/polymer scaffold was washed with ethanol followed by deionized water, and its dye removal efficiency was subsequently measured. As shown in Figure 15, the catalyst retained a high degradation efficiency during repeated use, although a slight decrease in performance was observed with successive cycles. The removal efficiency decreased from approximately 86% in the first cycle to 81% in the second cycle, and further to 73% in the third cycle. This gradual reduction in activity can be attributed to the partial accumulation of residual dye molecules on the catalyst surface, which may occupy active sites and hinder light absorption, thereby reducing the generation and migration of photoinduced charge carriers.
